items.title: The Pay Dirt
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
You can pay me now or you can pay me later. You can pay layaway, you can pay on credit, you can pay out of pocket, you can pay through the nose, you can pay an arm and a leg, you can pay dues, respects, dearly, heed, homage, lip service, compliments, cash on the barrelhead, the piper, peanuts, under the table, over the table, the ultimate price, or you can gladly pay me Tuesday. In the shadow of an election that was all about affordability, it seems like the last thing you need is a new way to pay. But agentic AI is here, and one of its supposedly excellent features is that it creates a new way to separate you from your money, and you don’t even have to be part of the process. You give the agent your credit card or banking info, and it will go out and manage transactions for you. That might sound like a big leap for consumers, but it’s a bigger leap for those on the receiving end of those payments (United Airlines is the latest company to ban AI agents), and an even bigger leap (and concern) for the industry that has been built over decades to manage those transactions. “Meta’s Muse, Instinct and other personal AI assistants have been empowered in recent weeks to make purchases on behalf of cardholders, marking new steps toward a potential future where consumers no longer need to initiate a purchase or press ‘buy’ at checkout. That is generating buzz and excitement about AI bots’ ability to create a new world order in payments. But inside banks and other payments companies and merchants, worries abound about the implications and whether bots will lead to elevated cases of fraud and returns, and open new legal risks. Early camps are already being formed.” (Gift Article): AI bots are using credit cards. Banks are racing to keep up. (alt link). “The systems that power payments today are built on byzantine rules, fraud protections, federal laws and network and bank fees that aren’t intended for robots. This ecosystem has long been in a state of constant tension between merchants, networks that set fees and rules, and card issuers that extend credit to consumers. Move one piece or change one fee even by a cent and the impact can quickly ripple into billions of dollars won and lost.” (I’d hold off on sharing your financial information with agents until things shake out and we know the systems are safe. There’s no need to turn your piggy bank into a guinea pig. You can pay me no mind, but excellent advice like this is why they pay me the big bucks.)

The fallout from the Nvidia story continues to take a toll on our psyches (and our portfolios). From (Gift Article): ‘I’m a Piece of Sh-t’: Jensen Huang’s Last Hours as Nvidia CEO. (With that kind of self-contempt, he should really consider writing a daily newsletter). From Stephen Witt in the (Gift Article): I Wrote Jensen Huang’s Biography. Here’s What Led to His Downfall. “When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it ‘The Thinking Machine.’ The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: ‘The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine.'”

+ As much as this is a business story and a corporate leadership lesson, the more we learn, the more we’ll realize that this is first and foremost a political scandal of Trumpian proportions. It goes right to the top, so someone on the way up has gotta take the fall. And anyone following the leaks can see the knives are out for the commerce secretary. Howard Lutnick under pressure over alleged lack of action. (The one good thing about this administration is that no matter who gets punished for something, they deserve it.)

+ “In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China.” But not until Trump loaded up on Nvidia stock. (You just grab them by the portfolio. When you’re president, they just let you do it.)

+ “One lesson of the Jensen Huang scandal is that policy makers gave extraordinary influence to technology executives whose commercial interests did not always align with American interests. His departure offers a rare opportunity to rethink the assumptions that have underpinned AI strategy for the past two years, address mounting concerns about the technology, and establish a new approach that protects both American AI leadership and public safety.” Thomas Wright in (Gift Article): The Jensen Huang Scandal Should Change Everything. Don’t get your hopes up. is doing a lot of work in that headline.

+ And if you missed it yesterday, I covered everything from the data center-sized portfolio losses, to the megawatt-powered affairs, to the unfair hit to the leather-wearing community: The Honey Trapdoor.

“Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself. The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.” A very interesting analysis about how the pathetic jerks at Fox News can spoil anything, even something as awesome and uplifting as the WNBA. Melanie Walsh with Jan Diehm in : Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA? This is about one sport, but it’s really about the way Fox News covers everything, and it will help explain where your crazy uncle got the ideas he’ll be sharing over Thanksgiving dinner.

Black Doves on Netflix, starring Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw, is like The Diplomat, meets Slow Horses, meets John Wick. It’s fun and fast-paced, and season two is better than season one (especially the addition of Ambika Mod).

+ In a follow-up to his excellent novel , Chad Harbach returns to the fictional campus of Westish College in his new and excellent novel, The Brightness. As Tom Perrotta says, “The Brightness is a monumental campus novel, full of smart and mercurial characters who feel as real as your own roommates.” (I swear, my freshman year college roommate was the president of the Berkeley Young Republicans. I once accidentally walked in on him and his girlfriend having sex. And I’ve been a Democrat ever since…)

“A river boat with over 100 passengers was struck on Friday by a much larger tanker ship, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River near the French Quarter.” The video and images from the scene are crazy. Rescue operations are underway. Here’s the latest.

+ A One Point Five Alarm Fire: “Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.” At this point, 1.5 is a pipe dream (and the temperature inside that pipe just set a record). A Key Paris Agreement Goal Is Dead. What Now?

+ After the warnings about AI destroying humanity, it was good old email that overpowered the system. A negative Outlook: Microsoft scrambles to fix email outage. “Very little is known so far about what is behind the outage, but Microsoft has attributed it to an ‘elevated load,’ or servers becoming overstretched. The tech giant assured users it was doing everything it could to fix the problem.” (I’d write an inappropriate pun about elevated loads, but I’m spent after a week of Nvidia jokes.)

+ “Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader, setting up a clash among Democrats just as they were celebrating their new majority.” (Infighting is Dems celebrate!)

+ Muting the Executioner’s Song: The excellent Bryan Stevenson in the (Gift Article): “The death penalty in America is not about whether people deserve to die for the crimes they commit; it is about whether our imperfect governments deserve to kill. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation last week of all of California’s 548 death sentences to life imprisonment without parole is a remarkable act of moral leadership.”

+ “Matt Lambert, a former emergency room physician and health care technology executive, shot five people and then himself on Thursday in D.C., apparently motivated by a bitter, ongoing and all-consuming legal dispute with the Metropole Condominium Association and the building’s property manager.” Michael Brice-Saddler in : What the Logan Circle Shooter Told Me.

items.title: The Honey Trapdoor
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
Jensen Huang had sex with multiple partners, but somehow my portfolio got screwed. When it comes to Nvidia, I got in early. And I stayed in. I’m not a promiscuous trader who goes in and out, in and out. And until this week, that loyalty had paid off. Like millions of stock owners, I wish I had pulled out earlier. In fairness, nobody thought the AI’s most engorged bubble would ultimately be popped like a cheap condom by the most human of desires. I still have no idea how a guy at the center of the company at the center of the industry at the center of the global economy had the vigor and spare time to juggle numerous affairs (not to mention Donald Trump’s ego). This guy was managing the most important company in the world while managing multiple romantic partners. I’ve seen 100 megawatt data centers that burn less energy. What was he trying to do, run for president? Seriously, if Huang had any more sex out of wedlock, he’d have to rename his company X. Everyone knows the number one rule in business is that you don’t have more partners than your company. I know this seems like a lot of cheap jokes, but after this week’s hit to my portfolio, I can no longer afford the expensive ones. And I’m not the only one. Everyone had Nvidia in their portfolios. And now the thrill is gone. And so is the trill (several of them, actually). I can’t remember if it was Warren Buffett, Milton Friedman, or John Maynard Keynes who said, “Don’t tap that if it will tap the market cap.” Now, Nvidia board members are left to Purell themselves as they feverishly search for a new leader to replace their supposedly irreplaceable old one, who just issued his resignation (although, I’m guessing the board pressed Ctrl-Shift-Esc before Huang pressed Command-Q).

+ Until today, the government was telling us that we can’t drive a Polestar or buy a DJI drone, but it’s fine if Nvidia sells chips to China. And the tech industry that has been telling us that we need to risk our very existence to stay ahead of the Chinese in the AI race initially tried to brush off Huang sharing secrets with a spy as no big deal. Up is down and wrong is right in the age of corruption. Jensen Huang’s resignation means the full story is probably a lot worse than what we already know. It also suggests that there are still lines that can’t be crossed (except when it comes to the administration, whose involvement in this is likely a bigger scandal than the scandal). Now comes the hardest part. Finding a new AI CEO whom people trust when AI CEOs have spent so much time convincing us they’re not to be trusted. Whoever gets the gig is going to have some big shoes — and a lot of little leather jackets — to fill. Trump says that Tim Apple should become Timvidia. But Trump himself is heavily implicated in this disaster. I’d rather see Tim Cook replace him. (If Cook says no to Nvidia, maybe Trump will suggest Dana White for the job.)

+ Meanwhile, the Justice Department has launched several investigations into purported honey-trapping spy Alice Huang. But the people at the very top of the administration were warned about her a long time ago.

+ “It has been a hard week, even for the thick-skinned. The news that Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence regards as a Chinese spy, has shaken not only Silicon Valley and geopolitics. It also has been an earthquake for the leather-jacket-wearing community.” Jensen Huang Betrayed the Leather Jacket Community. You can run, but you can’t rawhide.

There was a joke going around the internet that the reason it was taking so long to get the final election numbers from Mississippi is because they have to count, One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, Three Mississippi. Whatever took so long, it was worth the wait. Scott Colom’s “shocking upset victory in a state where Donald Trump won by 23 points in 2024 is even more remarkable considering Mississippi’s history. This was the state where Jim Crow was the most violent and repressive. It was where Emmett Till was lynched, Evers was assassinated, and the young civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan. There were 581 documented lynchings during the Jim Crow era, more than any other state.” Mississippi Elects Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction. “Before the passage of the Voting Rights Act, only 6.7 percent of eligible Black voters were registered to vote in Mississippi. Now, more than 60 years later, it was Black voters who turned out in record numbers to rewrite the history books, motivated in part by a new struggle to protect voting rights.”

+ “It was Mr. Hudson’s father who was initially cast in the campaign ad mocking a suggestion from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, that Mississippi residents pick another type of protein to avoid rising beef prices. When the elder Mr. Hudson balked at a script that would require him to utter profanity on camera, his son volunteered.” The Man at the Center of Scott Colom’s Protein Ad. (And shee-it, that ad helped change history.)

“These settlement numbers, reported for the first time, provide a rare glimpse into what the companies are willing to pay to avoid high-profile trials with teen users — and the looming financial risk such cases present. Roughly 9,800 personal injury cases are pending in state and federal court against Meta, Google’s YouTube, Snap Inc. and TikTok Inc.” (Gift Article): The Confidential Payments Meta and TikTok Made to Addicted Teens. “Seven confidential deals with young plaintiffs ranged from $2 million to $2.5 million. And the remaining personal injury lawsuits could expose the companies to billions of dollars in liability.”

“Air travel has become so safe in large part because of a profound commitment from the people in charge to learn from tragedies — what aviation experts call ‘lessons written in blood’ … But the Trump administration has displayed an extraordinary unwillingness to learn new lessons, and in some cases it seems to be unlearning the old ones.” James Fallows in the (Gift Article): Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?

+ Nothing to Write Home About: “The last time sales were this low was August 2010 when the economy was still reeling from the housing bust and the recession that followed.” (Gift Article): Home Sales in October Plummet to 16-Year Low.

+ “Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded the soldier who reprimanded him and members of his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal on Thursday.” (He must have been embarrassed to award someone he’d ordinarily fire.) After hearing voices and laughter, Specialist Iglesias of The Old Guard yelled, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

“​In its glory days, the S.S. United States was fast, luxurious and all but indestructible. As the ocean liner’s designer, William Francis Gibbs, liked to ​say, ‘You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her, and you can’t catch her.’ And he was right, up to a point. On Wednesday one of the greatest ships to sail the seas made its final journey, 180 feet down to the bottom of the ocean.​” The S.S. United States, a Historic Supership, Sinks to the Ocean Floor. But the metaphor doesn’t stop there. It was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico…

items.title: Everybody's Working for the Weakened
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
The new Dem majority hasn’t even been sworn in and the White House is already threatening to investigate the investigators. “The White House’s top lawyer is threatening a criminal investigation of Democrats for conducting what he alleges are illegitimate investigations into the executive branch — a stark escalation from the Trump administration as congressional Democrats prepare to launch an oversight onslaught when they assume the majority in January.” So the lawbreakers are threatening to go after the lawmakers. That doesn’t seem like the way it’s supposed to work, especially after an election when voters made it pretty clear that they are tired of the corruption. But while the Congress has the backing of a massive election win, the White House has something in its gold-leafed corner. A thoroughly decimated and corrupted Justice Department. And sadly, that’s a pretty big card to be able to play. “When the Justice Department has inserted itself between citizens denied their equal rights and the forces denying those rights, it has been a potent use of the U.S. government. Equally, though, when the Justice Department has inserted itself on the side of those denying others their rights, it has been a force multiplier for powerful interests. Short of the U.S. military, there is no greater coercive power that is brought to bear by the government against its citizens.” Rachel Maddow in (Gift Article): The Collapse of America’s Most Consequential Institution. “Over the course of its century and a half of existence, the Justice Department has been noble; it has been feckless; it has been corrupt. But now, in the midst of a full-fledged authoritarian challenge to the constitutional republic, the Justice Department has entered a whole new phase it has not been through before. It’s a phase you might call ‘gone’: missing, presumed dead.” Of course, a little more than a week ago, we could have made the same pronouncement about Congress.

+ The White House and the Justice Department will make it as difficult as possible to investigate the nefarious behavior that took place in broad daylight. Jim Himes is the point person when it comes to uncovering what took place (way) behind the scenes. (Gift Article): Top Democrat Vows Oversight of C.I.A.’s Use of Covert Action. “The incoming Democratic chairman of the House Intelligence Committee is promising to scrutinize the C.I.A.’s ‘extremely aggressive’ use of covert actions since President Trump returned to office, part of a broader effort to conduct renewed oversight of American spy agencies next year … His committee, he added, will also examine donations to Mr. Trump’s various construction projects in Washington from defense and intelligence contractors, and investigate whether intelligence analysts have been pressured to write reports that align with the objectives of senior officials in the Trump administration.” In other words, Jim Himes and his committee are going to be awfully busy digging through what could be a sea of awfulness. (Full disclosure: I know Jim Himes. He’s exactly the person you want on the job.)

“There will be parades and marching bands. Flag-waving and wreath-laying. Politicians will make speeches, friends will raise glasses and civilians will observe moments of silence. All to honor America’s service members, now and forever. But for those who have lost loved ones overseas in the Iran war, which has been waged since Feb. 28, this Veterans Day comes with a heaviness that only military families can fathom, and that will grow only more difficult as they face their first holiday season without their sons and daughters, siblings and spouses.” For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss. “Military families are navigating feelings of grief, pride and anger, as well as seeking answers about the deaths of their loved ones.”

+ We don’t usually associate casualties of war with the people working on the frontlines of our cyber agencies. But it turns out that job is proving to be increasingly deadly. (Gift Article): More Suicides at Spy, Cyber Agencies Scrutinized by Congress. “There is a lot of stress that a lot of us overlook because we think cyber is away from the front, and physically that’s accurate but intellectually and emotionally it’s inaccurate.”

“‘This was an audience we always thought might be lost to their small screens,’ said Paul Dergarabedian, head analyst of marketplace trends at Rentrak, a box-office data service. ‘But I think younger Gen Z audiences are particularly interested in those more handmade, tactile experiences, and going out to the movies is one of them. I think this is going to build on itself … The whole idea of moviegoing has become so cool.” (Gift Article): The Rise of the Gen Z Cinephile.

“In states that have seen reproductive access drastically curtailed since the end of Roe v. Wade, newly empowered Democratic governors and lawmakers could repeal abortion restrictions, codify new protections, and work toward enshrining reproductive freedom in state constitutions. Democratic attorneys general could stop enforcing draconian laws that threaten abortion providers and helpers with prosecution and reject efforts to criminalize pregnancy loss.” The Democratic Tsunami Is a ‘Sea Change’ for Reproductive Rights.

+ “Trump saw Russian diesel as a way to lower sky-high prices for the fuel, which contributed to rising consumer costs in the U.S. in the run-up to the midterm elections. But the diverted ships show U.S. oil companies are reluctant to handle the cargoes of Russian diesel because of the potential legal and reputational consequences.” (Gift Article): Trump’s Plan to Import Russian Diesel Stalls on the High Seas.

+ “Ollie Ballinger, an open-source researcher and lecturer, uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts around the world. But he says pressure from the government has prompted private companies to restrict access to images of places it may not want the public to see.” An video report: The View From Space the U.S. Government Doesn’t Want You to See.

+ “While Mr. al-Saadi is being held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, his communications with outsiders have been severely restricted. He has been shackled and held in a special housing unit often reserved for high-profile inmates … But while speaking by phone with his mother and sister over the summer, Mr. al-Saadi delivered coded messages about a forthcoming plot.” Failed Plot to Attack U.K. Base Used by U.S. Was Directed From New York Jail. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest official to be forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety.

+ Chipping Away at the Story: “A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington’s efforts to curb China’s access to advanced technology.” Plus, tracking how Jensen Huang changed his stance on China. Huang should be investigated. But so should the people (including the top person) in the White House who enabled him.

+ “The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.”

Well, well, well, it looks like we finally picked the week to stop sniffing glue. “Doctors in Belgium detailed a man in his 40s who developed a strange lesion in his lungs after accidentally inhaling superglue. Thankfully, the lesion wasn’t cancerous as originally feared and appears to have caused no harm, but it’s stuck around in his lungs for at least nine years.”

items.title: God and the Big Bang
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
I was tasked with selecting a new stain color for my house shingles, which was relatively traumatic because I have a history of spending an inordinate amount of time making decisions; a process that tends to be followed by a lifetime of regret. I recently spent about 30 hours researching a power adapter and dongle system to simultaneously charge my MacBook and Kindle. How was I going to choose a color for the entire exterior of my house before El Niño hits? I did what most modern internet users would have done. I used AI. I took photos of my house and then had AI show me how it would look stained in the various sample colors my painter suggested. Like many AI experiences, this one was pretty fulfilling and even delightful. But when I think about the AI industry, like millions of other Americans, I have almost exclusively negative vibes. Why does this technology cause such a disconnect between our experiences and our feelings? As I’ve mentioned, I think this is partly due to a broad and growing disconnect between what people want and what AI CEOs think people want. But even more than that, there’s a disconnect between how consumers think of AI (as a new form of super-powered search that finally brings the promise of AskJeeves to fruition) and how AI leaders think of it: As a god. Jaron Lanier explains the disconnect. “This disapproval is unfortunate and unnecessary. It does not arise from the technology itself. It is a reaction to the insular culture surrounding A.I., a culture that is dictating how this innovation is packaged, how it is sold and how it is understood. Words have a way of filtering into actions, as when some of us in Silicon Valley callously treat places where we want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. We technologists are sabotaging ourselves, but it is hard to find a sane focus from inside the intensity and elite isolation of this bubble. Americans are not rejecting A.I. They are rejecting the way Silicon Valley is defining it for them.” (Gift Article): I Am a Silicon Valley Pioneer. We Are Sabotaging Ourselves. (The irony here is that the thing consumers really dislike the most about this new technology is the people. And you can’t really blame them.) “There is an explanation for why some tech leaders, so seemingly worried about an extinction-level event, are plunging ahead with A.I. development: Mankind’s survival, while important to many of them, is less critical than building something they believe to be not only conscious but godlike. A substantial portion of the A.I. community, in celebrating this belief, is quick to support any action or statement that reinforces the idea that the technology is like a deity. They might call for regulation, but only in specific ways — perhaps by deploying more A.I. to control A.I. — that adore the technology’s powers. It is that adoration that is nonnegotiable.” I don’t know about you, but I’m not about to bow down at the altar of a new technological overlord. At least not until I see how my shingles turn out.

+ Which brings us to AI’s big bang… (Gift Article): The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? The stock is way down, the FBI and the newly empowered Dems are looking into the issue, and the Information reported that “CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with alleged spy Alice Huang dates back to 2023 and enabled Chinese companies to acquire $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips.” Here’s the latest. God only knows how this shakes out.

+ As I wrote yesterday: The enduring stamina of the notion that the carnal is greater than the kernel, that ramming overides the ram, and that the dong is greater than the dongle, provides yet another reminder that the key risk factors presented by the AI boom are the humans behind it. And, in this case, it’s a human in the center of a circular economy. Circular Jerk.

Pete Hegseth has declared war on those who want him impeached. That said, he tends to lose wars. “Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday cast the impeachment effort against him as a slanderous attempt by a single disgruntled Republican to damage President Trump, as House G.O.P. leaders said a procedural vote would come in a matter of hours. Democrats are expected to support removing him from office, and there may be enough Republican backing to imperil his leadership of the Pentagon.” It doesn’t help to be bad at your job and deeply hated. “Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral who won a seat in Congress last week after being fired by Pete Hegseth, has lent her support to lawmakers attempting to impeach the defense secretary, saying that he had committed ‘probably plenty’ of offenses to warrant his ouster.” Meanwhile, “Trump posted on social media that he gives Hegseth an ‘A’ PLUS PLUS PLUS’ for his remarks.” (I wonder if Hegseth can bring a Plus Plus Plus One to his impeachment…)

While we’re on the topic of grade inflation, the (Gift Article) has a piece on The Parents Suing Schools Because Their Kids Got Bad Grades. “Time was when parents disciplined children for bringing home bad marks. Today, they often take a more adversarial approach, educators say, leaning on teachers and administrators to change grades in disputes that can even spill into court. Ever since remote learning brought classrooms into living rooms during the pandemic, U.S. parents have grown more involved in and less enchanted with schools, according to numerous surveys. That includes scrutinizing how teachers evaluate their children. Four in 10 American teachers report facing pressure from moms and dads to change grades.”

“President Claudia Sheinbaum drew a firm line barring U.S. forces from operating on Mexican soil. But in a northern border state, one local partner quietly helped the agency build a foothold.” From life imitating art to life imitating a Netflix series. (Gift Article): The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico. “For more than six months, Mr. Zuany shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations, according to nine officials and law enforcement officers in Mexico and the United States. In return, officials said, Mr. Zuany’s U.S. visa was reinstated. Then, in April, a truck carrying two C.I.A. officers drove off a cliff, killing all four passengers. The crash blew the C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua and set off a national scandal.”

“After years of economic turmoil and droughts, the U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to its smallest level in 75 years. The supply shock is driving up steak and hamburger prices at grocery stores and restaurants to record highs—conditions that could last well into the next decade, given how long it takes to replenish a herd.” (Gift Article): Why High Beef Prices Are Here to Stay. (It will be interesting to see how the beef price crisis impacts public health.)

+ “For nearly a century, the United States has been the global leader in cultivating young scientists, training them at the nation’s vast network of universities and harnessing their talents to ensure American dominance in research and innovation. But now that Ph.D. pipeline is in turmoil.” Young Talent Fueled American Scientific Dominance. Now It’s Disappearing. (The midterms were great. But it will take years and years to undo the damage of Trumpism across many sectors.)

+ “At a time when the rich are walling themselves off from both society and ­reality—building apocalypse bunkers in New Zealand, buying gated homes in Miami and Newport Beach—there’s one major problem with their escapist fantasies: other rich people.” An insane, multi-year drama between billionaires that revolves around the person who was working in a tennis pro shop. This is, at least in part, a story about people who live for conflict. : Clash of the Titans.

+ “British writer M. John Harrison won the Booker Prize for fiction on late Monday for ‘The End of Everything,’ a satirical dystopian novel whose themes of ‘catastrophe and apocalypse’ chime with our uneasy times. It’s the first work of science fiction to take the prestigious $67,000 literary award.”

+ With So Much New Blood in the Senate, the Average Age Is Falling… To 63.

items.title: Circular Jerk
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
In 2026, there are thousands of massively scaled data centers across the world, and guys still think with their dicks. The enduring stamina of the notion that the carnal is greater than the kernel, that ramming overides the ram, and that the dong is greater than the dongle, provides yet another reminder that the key risk factors presented by the AI boom are the humans behind it (or in front of it, to the side of it, or whatever else you’re into). And thus, we found ourselves bracing for the global market response to news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair. Now, the idea that a tech CEO would upload his firmware into multiple devices is hardly breaking news, but in this case, at the risk of getting too graphical, Huang installed his processing unit into the wrong hosting facility. It looks like he may have been honey-trapped by a Chinese operative. This is big news because of national security, the global AI race, and Nvidia’s technological and financial prowess—and their circular deals—that place the mega-company smack dab in the middle of the AI economy, which is smack dab in the middle of the everything economy. Nvidia’s board, which denies that any damaging spying was done, has launched an internal investigation. But what, really, can be done? “Over the past four years, Jensen Huang has become the maestro of the artificial intelligence boom and its most essential billionaire executive. Nvidia, the company he co-founded in 1993, controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the big artificial intelligence projects that are driving the U.S. economy. That dominance has made Mr. Huang one of the wealthiest people in the world, as well as an ally of President Trump.” (Gift Article): Is Jensen Huang Too Powerful to Be Punished by Nvidia? That’s another way of asking if he’s too big to fail. But this is hardly a time for braggadocio.

+ Trump immediately backed Jensen Huang (Huang stands accused of simultaneous infidelity and treachery. In Trumpworld, that practically qualifies him for a Presidential Medal of Freedom). But, in a twist that will surprise no one, the Trump administration could be heavily implicated in this scandal. It turns out that some inside the administration have been worried about this issue for a while. Just not the top person. Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy. “Mr. Rubio’s involvement in warning administration officials about the situation has not been previously reported. It highlights how concerns about the relationship and the spying were known to senior officials even as Mr. Huang, a pivotal figure in the explosive growth of A.I., remained an influential voice with Mr. Trump over policy on the issue.” Wait, it gets shadier. Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention. “Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year.”

+ So far, the tech and broader markets are holding up better than expected in light of this news. As for Nvidia, it saw about $330 billion cut from its market cap on Monday. I’m guessing most investors (and political observers) will see this as a buying opportunity.

“How do you summon up shame for so many years of shamelessness? … For some, it will be impossible, even embarrassing, to keep Trump at arm’s length. Vance, for example, who long ago likened Trump to Hitler and to ‘cultural heroin,’ is far too bound to the regime, too eager for a promotion, too memorable as MAGA’s highest-ranking smirk to bow out now. The vice president can pray that the Iran war is his party’s only problem, but the guy who promoted lies about Haitian immigrants eating dogs and cats, who publicly supported fatal Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids and who defended the most reviled attack ad in the 2026 midterms might want to try that ‘honest conversation’ with himself. One day you’re riding the Trump train; the next, you find yourself tied to the tracks.” (Gift Article): JD Vance Needs to Stop Trying. (Trump’s enablers like JD Vance are political versions of Bruce Willis in . They don’t realize they’re already dead.)

Even the losers get lucky sometimes. But luckily for betting apps and prediction markets, not very often. “It’s true that millions of people use them only occasionally, and only to have a bit of fun. But these people are of modest value to the companies. The least active two-thirds of licensed sportsbook gamblers account for just 2.7% of estimated revenue, according to a Bloomberg Businessweek analysis of almost 140,000 bettors across 29 states in 2024 and ’25. The more lucrative bettors are the small but growing cohort of gamblers exhibiting likely problem behavior. A classic symptom would be topping off their sportsbook account hundreds of times a year. Without these people, digital sportsbooks could lose about 60% of their revenue. That’s unlikely to happen: Of the people who place deposits into sportsbooks monthly, 1 in 5 will eventually do so daily, our analysis found.” (Gift Article): The Spiral.

“Location tracking might start, for younger kids, with an AirTag slipped into a backpack, jacket, or shoe. (Skechers now makes shoes with a dedicated compartment in the sole.) For kids old enough to have their own smartwatch or phone, the GPS is built right in—and so parents keep tracking them into adolescence and even beyond. Three-quarters of parents with teenagers ages 14 to 17 had access to their kids’ location data, according to one study. Even among college students, one-third were being tracked by their parents, according to another study, conducted in 2021 by Michaeline Jensen, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. Five years later, Jensen says, that number is even higher: More than half of college students are being tracked, per her unpublished data. In her own lab, she’s learned that even her graduate students continue to be tracked; she told me about one student, 29, who recently defended her dissertation but whose mom still checks—and calls about—her location.” (Gift Article): What Constant Surveillance Is Doing to Children. (I don’t have to actively track my kids’ location. They share my Uber account…)

+ How much can older generations screw up the world before the youth finally take to the streets? About this much. “Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.” ‘A global political awakening’: how Gen Z protests are sweeping the world.

+ The Vampire Strikes Back: America to Trump: “We couldn’t hate you more.” Trump to America: “Hold my Miller.” A Chief of Staff Who ‘Will Crack Skulls‘. “Where Wiles served as something of a guardrail—making sure Trump was fully briefed and that he understood the risks and pitfalls of any decision—Miller has played the role of an accelerant for a president who already has rash tendencies.”

+ “The College Football Playoff and ESPN have signed a five-year deal that will expand the field to 24 teams in 2027 with ESPN as the event’s continued broadcast partner.” This is in keeping with their usual M.O. Good for the bottom line. Bad for the game. (And I’m not just mad because even if they expand it to 124 teams, Cal still wouldn’t make it…)

+ “‘Imagine explaining a wellness darty to someone who went to college in 2012,’ Aydan Child, the 25-year-old Gainesville, Fla., resident wrote in a September TikTok post that quickly went viral. In the video, fraternity brothers can be seen running shirtless and holding Pilates poses in front of the Pi Kappa Alpha house at the University of Florida. The post prompted outrage from various corners of the internet in what amounted to a generational panic; millennials and Gen Xers expressed horror at the notion that today’s college kids are hyper-fit and totally sober. The New York Post called the photos ‘bone-chilling.'” (Gift Article): Cold Plunges, Fitness Pop-Ups: The Students Pushing Clean Living on Campus. (Marlon Brando whisper-voice: “The horror, the horror.”)

items.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
Since the midterms were largely about affordability and fairness, and featured a rejection of the nonstop, unregulated data center sprawl, it may be tempting for some to celebrate the idea that the hubristic AI industry finally got theirs. But they don’t get theirs without you getting yours. The rising tide of AI may not have lifted all boats, but the draining of economic enthusiasm around that industry could sink us all. It’s the AI economy, stupid. AI drives big tech and together they drive the entire economy. Stocks, bonds, credit markets, hedge funds, bank lending, stock portfolios, your retirement account, investments, venture capital … no part of our financial system, from Wall Street to Main Street to 21 Jump Street, would escape a bubble burst unscathed. “Any downturn in the AI industry, either in the buildout of its infrastructure or the valuations of its stocks, will reverberate far beyond Silicon Valley. Technology companies have dominated the stock market for years, but artificial intelligence has pushed the concentration to new heights. Tech now accounts for nearly half the value of the benchmark S&P 500 Index.” (Gift Article): AI Has Taken Over Every Corner of the Market.

Eugene Levy, John Candy, Catherine O’Hara, Martin Short, Rick Moranis … SCTV was a cult favorite that introduced a generation of mainstream stars. On Netflix, check out SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of.

+ My local sports radio station’s weekly interview with Warriors coach Steve Kerr is now sponsored by the Contra Costa Library (which is about all you need to know about the current economics of radio). Kerr was recently asked for a book rec (which I took and enjoyed). Check out (in general, or even from the Conta Costa Library) Liz Moore’s The God of the Woods, in which a teenager vanishes from her Adirondack summer camp. (And yes, they’re already filming the Netflix version…)

Killing the Death Penalty: “State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us. I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.” Gavin Newsom Commutes the Sentences of California’s 548 Death Row Inmates. It’s worth noting that California hasn’t executed anyone on death row since 2006. So this move won’t necessarily have a significant, tangible impact, but it will certainly have a political impact.

+ A Dollar Sign of Things to Come: “Whether prediction markets can accurately anticipate election results has become a key question after the midterms. An analysis by The New York Times, using statistical methods, found that for most of the midterm race, prediction markets performed no better than election forecasts, which produce odds using polling and other indicators instead of betting activity. But as Election Day neared, prediction markets performed better as forecasts and polling became stale.” How Accurate Were Prediction Markets at Picking Midterm Winners? (Aren’t most of the people betting on elections on the prediction markets using traditional election forecasters as their guide? I mean, they’re not just betting on a hunch.)

+ You Thought Your Fill Up Was Expensive: “After Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea and seized territory commanding the strategic Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint, the kingdom reached out to the group to see what it would take to arrive at a negotiated halt to the hostilities. The answer it got back: $51 billion.”

+ “It was a reflection on the warm embrace Brand, a comedian and actor, has received from prominent Trump administration officials and other leaders in Kennedy’s ‘Make America Healthy Again’ (Maha) movement, where Brand has used his star status to criticize vaccines and vaccine mandates.” Weeks before rape conviction, Russell Brand was featured speaker for Maha group allied with RFK Jr. (Well, it’s not exactly like MAGA is anti-rape…)

+ “We’re in the era of the ultralong movie. Some of this year’s biggest films, including ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’ run nearly three hours. With no intermissions, viewers have to hold it or risk missing crucial moments. They’re flocking to RunPee, an app that recommends the best times for bathroom breaks with synopses of what they’ve missed.” Hollywood’s New Superhero Is the Guy Who Tells Moviegoers When to Pee.

items.title: The World is Flat
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
I was recently visiting Harvard Square, where I was looking forward to showing my daughter around. But it quickly became clear that she would be the one giving me the tour (even though she had never been there before). Between social media and the ubiquity of chains, she knew all the places where we should look, eat, and drink, and thanks to her superior GPS skills, I ended up following her from place to place. My daughter had never been to this specific neighborhood. But she had definitely been there and done that. While standing on some street in some city, the Dutch Australian data scientist Lauren Leek explained the feeling: “What we see in front of us used to be culturally diverse. Now it is culturally generic. Most of what we see is the big chains we see everywhere. It creates a sense of placelessness. We could be anywhere.” (Gift Article): Why Does Culture Feel So Monotonous? A Walking Tour Reveals the Math. “Leek recently posted a Substack article, with the headline ‘Temperature Zero for Culture: Why Everything Is Starting to Look the Same,’ that analyzed the ‘flattening’ effect that predictive algorithms have had on music, movies, hospitality and almost every aspect of today’s consumer culture … Taking 640 shopping streets in London as a test case, Leek used advanced data-analysis tools to examine how predictive algorithms have helped create what she calls a homogeneous ‘monoculture’ in which, she writes in her Substack post, ‘we lose the ability to tell the difference between what people wanted and what the system made easy to want.'” (I’m thinking of taking my daughter back to the street where I grew up. I could use a tour guide.)

The heart wants what the heart wants. And it wanted something very different deep in the heart of Texas. The adage that everything is bigger in Texas definitely held up during Tuesday’s election, when an epic blue wave swept across the state and proved (in a shocking manner) that those who assumed that Texas would be forever red were all hat and no cattle. Consider that James Talarico “got 4,397,474 votes in early voting—more than the 4,249,373 votes that his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General James Paxton, received overall.” From Rachel Monroe in : The Night That Texas’s Seemingly Unchangeable Republican Identity Vanished. “Last night, I drank tequila and exchanged stunned, giddy texts with friends back home, as it became increasingly clear that something extraordinary was happening. Paxton and Abbott were losing, but so was Dan Patrick, the lieutenant governor, who fought to install the Ten Commandments in every public-school classroom in the state; and Don Huffines, the comptroller, who has equated abortion with murder; and Bo French, the candidate for railroad commissioner, who once asked on X whether Muslims or Jews were a bigger threat to the country. The whole statewide G.O.P. apparatus—men who felt so secure in their power that they had nearly persuaded me to accept their inevitability—was teetering. Before yesterday, Texas had not elected a Democrat to statewide office in thirty-two years; now, nearly every key position will be held by a Democrat.” (I can’t wait to see how the characters on Landman react to all of this.)

+ “Elon Musk warned that Talarico would usher in the end of the American experiment. Ted Cruz said that “if Texas falls, everything changes.” Texas has fallen now, in almost every conceivable way. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats are poised to flip all 17 statewide offices that were on the ballot and take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2002. They could net one seat in Congress from a map Republicans just redrew to flip five. Democrats went into Election Day cautiously optimistic. They ended it with the single most shocking set of results, at scale, that I have seen in my lifetime.” Tim Murphy in : The Texas Miracle.

“The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing ‘billions of location data points.’ … The Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that law enforcement agencies must obtain a warrant from a judge to obtain location data from telecommunications companies. But the Justice Department has since argued that the principle does not apply to location data that agencies purchase from commercial sources, and Webloc users now include US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, at least two branches of the US military, and more than a dozen American police forces.” (Gift Article): Ads in Popular Apps Give Police a Powerful Tool to Spy on Users.

“The Korean government has a K-pop contract template that guarantees the right to education and to physical and mental health. The NewJeans contracts stripped away that language. The contracts banned such behavior as having an ‘insincere attitude,’ entering ‘inappropriate romantic relationships’ or criticizing the record label. The agreements included steep exit clauses and allowed the label to sell NewJeans music after the end of the deal, while slashing payments to the band. And it gave the label the right to use A.I.-generated NewJeans voices indefinitely.” (Gift Article): Secret Deals Reveal K-Pop’s Firm Grip on a Top Girl Group.

(Gift Article): “Americans’ vote for candidates and ballot measures to ban or slow data-center development could rein in AI’s rapid growth and become a big business problem for the companies on the edge of technological progress. It also threatens to hobble an AI boom powering the U.S. economy.” (Data center contempt is part of a broader distrust of AI, specifically, and big tech more broadly. Election results aside, tech companies have to address these issues.) Meanwhile, the day after the election, the market soared. The day after that, things turned upside down.

+ JD Vance is trying to save someone from the blue wave: JD Vance. “The vice president and 2028 hopeful is desperately trying to evade responsibility for the GOP’s bloodbath this week—by laying all the blame on his boss.” (To establish himself as the GOP frontrunner in 2028, JD Vance has to do two things: One, distance himself from Trump. Two, stop being a charisma-free, hateable, evil, boring, awful in every way, piece of garbage loser who is immediately despised by all who encounter him. It should be interesting to watch.)

+ “Speaking at the White House, the first lady expressed hope that the six-day ceasefire around Oleshky would inspire a peace ‘more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,’ before praising the ‘highly cooperative’ Russian and Ukrainian leaders for helping bring about the pause.” Is Melania now in charge of peace talks? Does her husband know? Last we checked, he was back in the ballroom. “Now envision chandeliers all over.”

+ “If passed by enough states, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would effectively nullify the Electoral College and, with it, the possibility of a candidate being elected president without winning the popular vote. Since the compact was introduced in 2006, 19 states have passed it, agreeing to assign their electoral votes to whichever candidate wins the national popular vote. That amounts to 222 of the 270 electoral votes that a candidate needs to win the presidential election.” Democrats Win Enough Seats Nationwide to End Electoral College.

+ Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for the second time in a week. “Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair’s Helsinki-Rome flight.”

+ Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault. The judge told Brand the consequence of the verdicts was a ‘significant custodial term.’ Here’s the latest from The Times.

+ “Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week.” Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayor’s race.

+ “Even as LIV Golf circled the drain in bankruptcy court, people around the league insisted that it had the means and vision to turn around the troubled outfit. Just last week, two-time major champion Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s most popular player, appeared on a podcast saying he was hopeful it could live forever.” (Or, maybe not.) LIV Golf Is Finished After Last-Ditch Revival Efforts Fail.
